item.title: Man killed, four injured in separate shootings in Balochistan; Quetta residents protest high gas bills
item.description: The deceased was identified as Shahjahan, son of Babul, who reportedly died at the scene, while his brother Imam Bakhsh sustained gunshot injuries. Both were subsequently taken to Teaching Hospital ...
item.content:encoded:
Man killed, four injured in separate shootings in Balochistan; Quetta residents protest high gas bills The deceased was identified as Shahjahan, son of Babul, who reportedly died at the scene, while his brother Imam Bakhsh sustained gunshot injuries. Both were subsequently taken to Teaching Hospital Turbat. ANI | Updated: 04-11-2026 21:01 IST | Created: 04-11-2026 21:01 IST

Representative Image (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

One man was killed and four others, including women and children, were injured in separate shooting incidents in Balochistan's Kech and Kohlu districts, while another man was found shot dead in Turbat, according to a report by The Balochistan Post (TBP). Citing local sources, TBP reported that Frontier Corps (FC) personnel allegedly opened fire on two brothers travelling on a motorcycle in the Bal Nigwar area of Dasht in Kech district. The deceased was identified as Shahjahan, son of Babul, who reportedly died at the scene, while his brother Imam Bakhsh sustained gunshot injuries. Both were subsequently taken to Teaching Hospital Turbat. According to the report, the authorities and district administration had not issued an official statement regarding the incident at the time of reporting. In a separate incident in Kohlu district, three people, including women and children, were injured after a vehicle came under fire. Local sources attributed the shooting to a government-backed armed group, TBP reported. However, further details about the incident and the condition of those injured were not immediately available. Meanwhile, the body of another man, identified as Asif, son of Barkat, was reportedly discovered with gunshot wounds at Kallag Cross on the M-8 highway in Turbat. Asif, a resident of Buleda, was found dead under circumstances that remained unclear, with the motive behind his killing yet to be established, according to TBP. In a separate report, TBP highlighted a protest by residents of Quetta, who blocked Samungli Road to demonstrate against allegedly excessive gas bills and incorrect meter readings. According to the report, protesters said unusually high bills had placed an additional financial burden on domestic consumers, creating serious difficulties for households already struggling with limited incomes. The demonstrators alleged that consumers were being asked to pay thousands and, in some cases, even hundreds of thousands of rupees in gas charges, making it difficult for ordinary families to meet the demands. The protesters called on the Sui Southern Gas Company (SSGC) and relevant authorities to conduct a transparent review of disputed bills, remove unjustified additional charges and provide financial relief to affected consumers. The demonstration also disrupted traffic along Samungli Road, causing inconvenience to commuters and other road users. (ANI)

item.title: US midterm elections: Democrats flip Nevada governor’s mansion, hold historic win in Wisconsin as GOP secures Nebraska Senate seat
item.description: In Nevada, The Associated Press projects that Democratic State Attorney General Aaron Ford will win the governor’s race, successfully flipping the executive seat for Democrats.
item.content:encoded:
US midterm elections: Democrats flip Nevada governor’s mansion, hold historic win in Wisconsin as GOP secures Nebraska Senate seat In Nevada, The Associated Press projects that Democratic State Attorney General Aaron Ford will win the governor’s race, successfully flipping the executive seat for Democrats. ANI | Updated: 04-11-2026 19:53 IST | Created: 04-11-2026 19:53 IST

Representative Image (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Key projection calls have determined major victories in high-stakes state and federal contests across the country. According to projections by ABC News, Democrat David Crowley will win the Wisconsin gubernatorial race. His historic victory makes him the state’s first Black governor. In Nevada, The Associated Press projects that Democratic State Attorney General Aaron Ford will win the governor’s race, successfully flipping the executive seat for Democrats. Meanwhile, in federal legislative races, The Associated Press projects that Republican Senator Pete Ricketts will hold his US Senate seat in Nebraska. Ricketts defeated independent challenger Dan Osborn, who has formally conceded the race. This comes amid a major political reversal in Washington, with US networks projecting that Democrats have secured control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the November 3 midterm elections. From Gina Hinojosa's breakthrough victory in the Texas gubernatorial race to Adam Hamilton's historic Senate win in Kansas and Rob Sand's gubernatorial triumph in Iowa, Democrats have registered gains across states that have traditionally favoured Republicans, while also making advances in key congressional contests. According to CNN, Democrat Hinojosa defeated Republican Governor Greg Abbott to become the first Latina governor of Texas, ending more than three decades of Republican dominance in the state's gubernatorial office.CBS News also projected Hinojosa's victory, reporting that Abbott had called to concede after losing his re-election bid. With 67 per cent of the votes counted, Hinojosa secured 3,994,529 votes, accounting for 57.1 per cent, while Abbott received 2,915,910 votes, or 41.7 per cent, according to CBS News. The 52-year-old state lawmaker and attorney will become the first Democrat elected governor of Texas since Ann Richards in 1990 and only the third woman to hold the office. Hinojosa, who represents an Austin district and is originally from Brownsville in the Rio Grande Valley, defeated Abbott, who had been seeking a fourth term after serving as governor since 2015. The Democratic breakthrough extended to the Texas Senate race, where James Talarico defeated Republican Ken Paxton, according to CBS News projections. With 58 per cent of ballots counted, Talarico had secured 58.1 per cent of the vote, against Paxton's 40.4 per cent. Following his victory, Talarico posted "Texas forever" on X. The developments in Texas are particularly significant, as Democrats have not won a statewide election in the state in more than three decades, making the results a notable departure from its recent Republican electoral record. Kansas also witnessed a historic political shift, with Democrat Adam Hamilton defeating Republican Senator Roger Marshall in the Senate race. The victory marks the first time in 94 years that Kansas will elect a Democrat to the US Senate, according to Fox News. Hamilton, a megachurch pastor, defeated incumbent Marshall in a contest where the Republican campaign faced difficulties in its final stages. Fox News reported that Hamilton gained support among independent and rural voters, contributing to the outcome. Another significant Democratic victory came from Iowa, where Democrat Rob Sand defeated Republican Zach Lahn in the gubernatorial election, according to CBS News projections. With 85 per cent of the votes counted, Sand secured 674,063 votes, representing 56.7 per cent, while Lahn received 513,948 votes, or 43.3 per cent. Iowa, once considered a competitive swing state, has increasingly leaned Republican in recent years. Sand's victory therefore adds another state to the list of traditionally conservative territories where Democrats have made electoral gains. The Iowa Senate contest also showed a Democratic advantage, with Josh Turek leading Republican Representative Ashley Hinson. CBS News assessed the race as leaning Democratic. With 90 per cent of the votes counted, Turek had received 635,000 votes, accounting for 50.9 per cent, while Hinson secured 573,706 votes, or 46 per cent, according to CBS News. Democratic gains were also visible in South Carolina, where Democrat Annie Andrews defeated Republican Darline Graham in the Senate race. Andrews' victory is notable as South Carolina voted for President Donald Trump by nearly 20 percentage points in the 2024 presidential election and has not elected a Democratic senator since 1998. Democrats also flipped the North Carolina Senate seat and retained their position in battleground Georgia. At the national level, US Networks projected that Democrats would reclaim control of the House of Representatives, opening the possibility of a significant change in the balance of power in Washington. The projected victory could put Democratic Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries on course to become the first African American Speaker of the House, although he would need to secure the necessary votes when the new Congress convenes in January. The projected Democratic takeover marks a significant setback for Republicans, who previously controlled both chambers, and is expected to give the opposition party greater powers to scrutinise Trump's administration and challenge his legislative agenda. A Democratic majority in the House would allow lawmakers to launch investigations, hold hearings and issue subpoenas concerning the administration, while control of the Senate would give Democrats greater influence over legislation, judicial confirmations and presidential appointments.(ANI)

item.title: Bangladesh: HRW flags political reprisals against academics, students over Hasina links
item.description: Human Rights Watch (HRW) has raised concerns over alleged political targeting of academics and students at public universities in Bangladesh over their purported links to former Prime Minister Sheikh ...
item.content:encoded:
Bangladesh: HRW flags political reprisals against academics, students over Hasina links Human Rights Watch (HRW) has raised concerns over alleged political targeting of academics and students at public universities in Bangladesh over their purported links to former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and her Awami League party, warning that dismissals, suspensions and restrictions imposed without due process could violate fundamental human rights. ANI | Updated: 04-11-2026 14:11 IST | Created: 04-11-2026 14:11 IST

Representative Image (File Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Human Rights Watch (HRW) has raised concerns over alleged political targeting of academics and students at public universities in Bangladesh over their purported links to former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina and her Awami League party, warning that dismissals, suspensions and restrictions imposed without due process could violate fundamental human rights. In a statement released on Tuesday, the international rights organisation said scores of university teachers and students had faced arbitrary disciplinary action over alleged support for Hasina's former government, which was toppled following student-led protests in 2024. HRW said such measures, if imposed for peaceful political beliefs or without ensuring due process, would violate internationally protected rights to freedom of expression and association. "Bangladesh has a long history of political debate in its universities, and only autocrats should fear such discourse, not a government formed following student protests," said Meenakshi Ganguly, Deputy Asia Director at Human Rights Watch. "Bangladesh needs to turn the page on the repression of the past, not repeat it whenever the ruling and opposition parties trade places," she added. According to HRW, the disciplinary measures include dismissals, suspensions, restrictions on teaching responsibilities and other academic activities. The allegations against the affected academics range from complicity in violence during Hasina's tenure and involvement in activities supporting the Awami League to alleged discrimination against students wearing Islamic clothing. The organisation also flagged the expulsion of hundreds of students allegedly affiliated with the Awami League, saying the measures had affected their right to education. HRW said it interviewed more than a dozen affected teachers, examined university correspondence and reviewed a televised discussion and social media footage as part of its investigation. Interviews with teachers and students also confirmed cases involving expulsions, cancellation of examination certificates and restrictions on access to university campuses. Citing media reports from August 2026, the organisation said at least 404 additional academics across 22 universities had been placed under investigation for their participation in a Telegram messaging group associated with the Awami League. A professor at a public university, whose identity was withheld for security reasons, told HRW that university authorities were targeting teachers allegedly aligned with the Awami League who had not supported the 2024 student movement. "What is happening now is that the university authorities are targeting with false allegations the group of teachers who are aligned to the Awami League and did not support the 2024 student movement," the professor said. "We are not allowed to go take classes, we cannot do research work, we cannot do anything," the professor added. The report highlighted disciplinary actions at several major public universities, including Dhaka University, Bangladesh Agricultural University and Sher-e-Bangla Agricultural University. At Dhaka University, authorities reportedly ordered 44 academics to stop working and restricted the teaching assignments of another 25 from September 2024, without what HRW described as a transparent or credible disciplinary investigation. Six academics were subsequently temporarily suspended, while investigations were initiated against another 14 teachers. At Bangladesh Agricultural University in Mymensingh, 12 academics were reportedly dismissed, suspended or removed from their positions, while another 34 faced demotions or restrictions on their activities following an investigation process that HRW said appeared inconsistent with the university's legally established disciplinary procedures. Similarly, at Sher-e-Bangla Agricultural University in Dhaka, 12 academics were temporarily suspended and another 10 removed from academic activities. Another 85 teachers were reportedly denied promotions. HRW said more than 20 public universities had been affected by such measures. The organisation also raised concerns over action against students. In March 2025, Dhaka University temporarily suspended 126 students and withheld their examination certificates after a fact-finding committee reportedly identified photographic, video or social media evidence suggesting their involvement in attacks on peaceful protesters. Police complaints also named another 277 students allegedly affiliated with the Awami League. However, HRW said the university had not taken formal disciplinary action against them, while students and teachers confirmed that some were staying away from campus over fears of arrest. The report also detailed the case of Professor Mashiur Rahman of Dhaka University's sociology department, who was instructed to stop academic and administrative work on September 25, 2024. Among the allegations against him was that he had opposed the 2024 protest movement during a television discussion. However, HRW said a video of the broadcast reviewed by the organisation did not show him making the alleged remarks. He was also accused of inciting genocide during a meeting at the Prime Minister's residence on August 3, 2024. Rahman told HRW that the meeting had been organised by the University Grants Commission and attended by vice-chancellors, and denied making the alleged statement. On August 31, 2026, university authorities recommended his permanent suspension, a decision he is appealing, according to HRW. The organisation also cited cases involving academics at Bangladesh Agricultural University, including Professor Purba Islam and Professor Yahia Khandoker, who were suspended over alleged support for Hasina during a pro-Awami League procession on August 4, 2024. HRW's review of footage of the procession found people walking across the university campus while chanting slogans, with no direct confrontations visible. The organisation said the footage did not establish the allegations of slogan-shouting against Professor Islam. Khandoker, meanwhile, maintained that he was with his family in Dhaka throughout the protest period and was not present at the university. The High Court stayed his suspension, although the Attorney General's Office is appealing the decision. The developments come against the backdrop of the political upheaval in Bangladesh in 2024, when hundreds of people were killed during a police crackdown on student-led protests in July and August, forcing Hasina to leave the country. The Awami League's activities were subsequently criminalised by the interim government in May 2025. Following the February 2026 election, the Bangladesh Nationalist Party returned to power. HRW also noted that three academics, including two who are in prison, had been convicted by the country's International Crimes Tribunal on crimes against humanity charges, while another was awaiting trial. Highlighting the importance of protecting academic freedom, Ganguly warned against using universities as instruments of political retaliation. "Any acts of revenge against people who peacefully supported the previous government would show that freedoms of speech and assembly are not protected," she said. "Universities should be places where people are free to express their views, not places where support is enforced for the government of the day," Ganguly added. (ANI)

item.title: “Netanyahu is toxic”: Israeli opposition leader warns of isolation and clash with US after midterms
item.description: Following the US midterm elections, Israeli opposition leader Yair Golan warned that Netanyahu's leadership risks international isolation. Meanwhile, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher ...
item.content:encoded:
“Netanyahu is toxic”: Israeli opposition leader warns of isolation and clash with US after midterms Following the US midterm elections, Israeli opposition leader Yair Golan warned that Netanyahu's leadership risks international isolation. Meanwhile, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf stated that the American vote reflects a rejection of war, as shifting congressional control reshapes foreign policy. ANI | Updated: 04-11-2026 13:55 IST | Created: 04-11-2026 13:55 IST

Israeli Democrats leader Yair Golan (Photo/Reuters). Image Credit: ANI

SHARE

Key Takeaways AI Summary

Analyzing article...

Following the US midterm elections, political figures across the Middle East have reacted sharply to the seismic shift in Washington's balance of power, warning of profound geopolitical repercussions. Israeli Democrats leader Yair Golan has issued a sharp critique of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, warning that his continued leadership risks severe diplomatic fallout and international isolation for Israel. Reacting to the political shift in the United States, Golan took to social media to argue that the election outcomes demonstrate deep bipartisan alienation, asserting that the results "reveal just how toxic Netanyahu is among both Democrats and Republicans". Warning of the geopolitical consequences, Golan cautioned that persisting with the current administration under Netanyahu and National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir could place the nation on a perilous trajectory, stating that their tenure "could lead Israel down a path of international sanctions, international isolation, and a clash with the U.S., our friend and most important ally". The opposition leader emphasised the necessity of a political reset to safeguard the country's strategic standing and long-term security. "Israel needs a government that will restore its standing in the world, promote long-term political-strategic arrangements, and ensure its security," Golan said. Contrasting two distinct national futures, he framed the current political juncture as a stark choice, “Netanyahu's Israel — 'Super Sparta', boycotted, backward, and isolated — or a strong, advanced, free, and secure Israel.” Declaring that “Netanyahu lost the elections,” Golan urged immediate domestic political action, stating, “He is dangerous to Israel. We have no time to waste. We must form a government of change now.” Meanwhile, Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf has also weighed in on the incoming election results, asserting that the electoral verdict demonstrates a clear rejection of conflict by the American public. Sharing his perspective on X, Ghalibaf stated, “Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message. If the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare.” These regional reactions unfold against the backdrop of the November 3 midterm elections, where vote tallies indicate that Democrats are poised to assume control of the US Congress, having secured the Senate and advanced across multiple seats in the House of Representatives. The sweeping legislative realignment follows a bruising electoral cycle in which domestic economic anxieties and foreign policy friction, notably the ongoing military engagement involving Iran, weighed heavily on voters. With all 435 House seats and 35 Senate positions contested, the unfolding results signal a profound shift in Washington's power dynamics, undercutting the Republican legislative majority and setting the stage for major political realignment. (ANI)
